title: Zaynab bint Jahsh
hook: the wives measure their hands to solve a riddle, and the answer turns out to be charity (Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Umm Salamah, who advised silence and asked to be named. Your line was: she asked, and it came. Did you ask your missing question? Day eight hundred twelve.

Who will be first? In Sahih Muslim, Aisha tells it. The Prophet had said to his wives that the one of them with the longest hand would be the quickest to join him after his death. So they measured their hands, side by side, to see whose was longest. It sounds like a party game: wives holding out their arms, comparing fingertips. And they missed what he meant. Today: Zaynab bint Jahsh.
screen: `WHO WILL FOLLOW HIM FIRST?` → `THE LONGEST HAND.` → `THEY MEASURED.`

segments.voice: The wives took the words of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, literally, and looked for the longest arm. But Aisha says the longest hand among them was Zaynab bint Jahsh's, because she used to work with her hands and give in charity. Tradition says she was the first of the wives to follow him in death. The riddle was never about length. It was about reach: how far a person's hands went toward others. In Arabic the phrase is atwalukunna yadan, the longest of you in hand. The report itself shows what a long hand meant: a giving one. Notice where her giving came from. Zaynab didn't only hand over what she had. She made things, the report says, and gave from the work of her own hands. Charity that has your fingerprints on it. Notice also who tells us this. Aisha and Zaynab were rivals in the household; the reports don't hide it. Yet it is Aisha who preserves Zaynab's best memory. In another report in Muslim, Aisha describes her as unmatched in her religion, in her fear of Allah, in truthfulness, in keeping ties of family, and in giving charity. And in the account of the slander against Aisha, Bukhari has Zaynab asked what she knew, and answering that she knew nothing but good of her. The two women spoke well of each other when it counted. The longest hands, it turns out, also reached across a rivalry.
screen: `THEY MEASURED THEIR HANDS.` · `SHE WORKED, AND SHE GAVE.` · `A LONG HAND IS A GENEROUS ONE.` · `RIVALS WHO SPOKE WELL OF EACH OTHER.` · then, large: `THE LONGEST HANDS.`

segments.voice: The practice: give with your own hands. Settle, and rest your hands open on your knees. Look at them. Breathe. Think of one thing those hands could make or do for someone else today. Bake something, mend something, write a note by hand, carry someone's bags, cook a meal to share. Not money from a screen. Something with your fingerprints on it. Choose one, and picture your hands doing it. If you pray, you can ask that your hands reach a little further. The bell holds the time.
Atwalukunna yadan, 'the longest of you in hand,' the riddle about reach, not length, that named Zaynab bint Jahsh, who gave from her own hands' work. Today's word.
Your line: the longest hands. Today, make or do one thing for someone with your own hands, and give it. Day eight hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the hadith of 'the longest hand' from Sahih Muslim when speaking of charity, and honor Zaynab bint Jahsh among the mothers of the believers for giving from the work of her hands.

original.note: Arabic: 'the longest of you in hand', the Prophet's words in Muslim.

trapdoor: what you thought: a riddle about whose arm was longest.
what it means: the longest hand was the most generous one, and it was Zaynab's.
what a scholar hears: Muslim 2452 names Zaynab; one version in Bukhari (1420) reads differently, and commentators discuss how to reconcile them.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2452 (the longest hand; Zaynab worked with her hands and gave charity)
Sahih Muslim 2442 (Aisha's praise of Zaynab's religion, truthfulness and charity)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; confirm.
Bukhari 1420's wording can be read as naming Sawdah; the script follows Muslim 2452 and the trapdoor mentions the difference. Keeper to check framing.
The marriage to Zayd and verse 33:37 are deliberately not covered.
'A long hand can mean a generous one' in Arabic usage: confirm.
Stress in the transliteration of atwalukunna yadan is approximate; confirm.

Editor: removed the invented wall from the hook and the claim that Muslim has the wives asking (that question is in Bukhari 1420); Zaynab dying first is now 'tradition says', since Muslim 2452 does not state it; cut an unsourced Arabic-usage claim; varied the opener.

Auditor: the word segment said the Prophet called Zaynab the longest in hand; in Muslim 2452 he names no one and Aisha identifies her, so it is now attributed to Aisha. Fork option no longer reintroduces the invented wall.
